title: Three ways to sail the Nile
standfirst: Every Nile cruise is shaped by its boat. Here are the three kinds still sailing between Luxor and Aswan, what each is like on board, and how to choose between them. [[up]]

sections.heading: The sailing dahabiya
paragraphs: A dahabiya is a two-masted sailing houseboat, the kind nineteenth-century travellers hired for the whole winter. Today’s dahabiyas have a handful of cabins, a shaded upper deck and a small crew who know their guests by name. They sail when the wind allows and are towed when it drops, and they moor at riverbanks and islands rather than town quays.

sections.heading: The motor cruise ship
paragraphs: Most Nile cruises are on motor ships: three to five decks, a restaurant, a lounge and usually a pool on the sun deck. They keep to set schedules, typically four nights upstream from Luxor to Aswan or three nights downstream, and moor at town quays, often several ships side by side.

sections.heading: The paddle steamer
paragraphs: A few historic paddle steamers still work the river, restored in period style. They are larger than a dahabiya and far smaller than a cruise ship, and they move at an unhurried pace that suits the scenery.

sections.heading: How to choose
paragraphs: If you want quiet, flexibility and a small group, look at dahabiyas. If you want facilities, a fixed programme and a lower starting price, a cruise ship fits. The comparison below shows the differences side by side, with figures from our vessel directory.

faqs.q: Which is the most comfortable way to cruise the Nile?
faqs.a: Comfort depends on the vessel more than the type. Large ships offer more facilities; dahabiyas offer space per guest and quiet. Our evaluation of each vessel scores cabins, service and hygiene separately.

faqs.q: Can I sail on a felucca?
faqs.a: Feluccas are small open sailing boats used for short trips, not overnight cruises. A felucca sail in Aswan is often part of a cruise programme.
